advances: Proves a direct unweighted second-moment lower bound for the actual closed-halfspace depths of a finite index measure at the exponential scale \(2^{-n}\), using only integer-midpoint quasiconcavity. It includes its exact formulation under the original squared-weight sampling law, its application to actual convex-body fiber volumes, and the Boolean-cube calibration. An exact odd-interval product body simultaneously disproves the proposed universal conversion from this moment divided by total mass to maximum ambient mixed-integer depth. The packet therefore establishes the index estimate and the precise limitation necessary for its use in the locked problem.
author: research-agent
external_sources: None. Accepted fact 488f0a583886b5fc supplies only the global log-concave extendability of actual positive-total-mass fiber tables, with the exact notation and zero-fiber applicability stated above. All index-depth estimates, parity counting, rank interpolation, sampling identities, and actual-body obstruction are proved here. No unavailable sandbox note is used as a premise.
proof:
For any proper closed halfspace containing a target \(\mathbf j\), translating its boundary parallel to itself until the boundary passes through \(\mathbf j\) gives a contained closed halfspace still containing \(\mathbf j\). Thus (2) equals the infimum over all containing closed halfspaces. The availability of a nonzero ambient normal follows from \(n\ge1\), even if \(D\) has smaller affine rank. In particular, for every \(\mathbf j\in D\), each admissible halfspace contains its atom, so \(w_{\mathbf j}\le\tau_w(\mathbf j)\le W\). Dividing every halfspace mass by the positive constant \(W\) proves the normalization in (2).

Fix \(t>0\). Let \(D_t=\{\mathbf i\in\mathbb Z^n:w_{\mathbf i}\ge t\}\) and \(N_t=|D_t|\). At nonempty levels define the counting depth \(d_t(\mathbf j)=\inf_{\mathbf u\ne\mathbf0}|\{\mathbf i\in D_t:\mathbf u\cdot(\mathbf i-\mathbf j)\ge0\}|\) and, for \(\mathbf j\in D_t\), the reflection count
\[
r_t(\mathbf j)
=|\{\mathbf i\in D_t:2\mathbf j-\mathbf i\in D_t\}|.
\tag{7}
\]
The reflected set contains \(\mathbf j\). All its other points split into disjoint pairs \(\{\mathbf i,2\mathbf j-\mathbf i\}\). Every containing closed halfspace contains \(\mathbf j\) and at least one endpoint of each pair, because their signed scalar products relative to the boundary through \(\mathbf j\) are opposites. Endpoints lying on that boundary cause no loss because the halfspace is closed. Therefore \(d_t(\mathbf j)\ge(r_t(\mathbf j)+1)/2\).

For each parity vector \(\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^n\), let \(N_{t,\epsilon}\) be the number of points of \(D_t\) in that parity class. Every ordered same-parity pair \( (\mathbf i,\mathbf k)\in D_t^2\) has an integer midpoint \(\mathbf j=(\mathbf i+\mathbf k)/2\). Hypothesis (1), applied at this level, puts that midpoint in \(D_t\). The correspondence \( (\mathbf i,\mathbf k)\mapsto(\mathbf j,\mathbf i)\) is a bijection onto the objects counted by \(\sum_{\mathbf j\in D_t}r_t(\mathbf j)\); its inverse is \( (\mathbf j,\mathbf i)\mapsto(\mathbf i,2\mathbf j-\mathbf i)\). This includes diagonal pairs exactly once. Cauchy-Schwarz on the \(2^n\) parity counts gives
\[
\sum_{\mathbf j\in D_t}r_t(\mathbf j)
=\sum_{\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^n}N_{t,\epsilon}^2
\ge\frac{N_t^2}{2^n}.
\tag{8}
\]
No completeness of \(D_t\) is used: its closure under integer midpoints is precisely the property needed in this bijection. Every halfspace has \(w\)-mass at least \(t\) times its count in \(D_t\), so \(\tau_w(\mathbf j)\ge t d_t(\mathbf j)\). Consequently
\[
\sum_{\mathbf j\in D_t}\tau_w(\mathbf j)
\ge\frac t2\left(\frac{N_t^2}{2^n}+N_t\right)
\ge\frac{tN_t^2}{2^{n+1}}.
\tag{9}
\]
At an empty level both sides are zero, so (9) holds for every \(t>0\).

We next pass from complete equal-weight blocks to all ranks. List the distinct positive weights in strictly decreasing order \(t_1>\cdots>t_M>0\). Write \(B_k=\{\mathbf j:w_{\mathbf j}=t_k\}\), \(N_0=0\), and \(N_k=|B_1|+\cdots+|B_k|=N_{t_k}\). On each interval \( (N_{k-1},N_k]\), define
\[
a(s)=t_k,
\qquad
b(s)=\frac1{|B_k|}\sum_{\mathbf j\in B_k}\tau_w(\mathbf j).
\tag{10}
\]
Set both functions to zero at zero and beyond \(N_M=|D|\). All these functions are nonnegative, bounded, and supported in a finite rank interval. The atom bound \(\tau_w\ge w\), finite summation, and Cauchy-Schwarz within each block yield
\[
\int_0^\infty a(s)\,ds=W,
\qquad b(s)\ge a(s),
\qquad
\int_0^\infty b(s)^2\,ds
\le\sum_{\mathbf j\in D}\tau_w(\mathbf j)^2.
\tag{11}
\]
For the last assertion, a block of size \(|B_k|\) contributes \((\sum_{B_k}\tau_w)^2/|B_k|\le\sum_{B_k}\tau_w^2\).

Put \(F(s)=\int_0^s b(u)\,du\). At the right endpoint of block \(k\), (9) gives \(F(N_k)\ge t_k N_k^2/2^{n+1}\). At the left endpoint of the first block, \(F(0)=0\) gives the needed bound exactly. For \(k\ge2\), apply (9) to the preceding level \(t_{k-1}\), obtaining
\[
F(N_{k-1})
\ge\frac{t_{k-1}N_{k-1}^2}{2^{n+1}}
\ge\frac{t_kN_{k-1}^2}{2^{n+1}}.
\tag{12}
\]
This explicitly supplies the left endpoint estimate; no estimate on a partial tie block is assumed. On the closed interval \([N_{k-1},N_k]\), the function \(F\) is affine. If \(s=(1-\theta)N_{k-1}+\theta N_k\), \(0\le\theta\le1\), the two endpoint estimates and convexity of \(s^2\) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
F(s)
&=(1-\theta)F(N_{k-1})+\theta F(N_k)\\
&\ge\frac{t_k}{2^{n+1}}
\bigl((1-\theta)N_{k-1}^2+\theta N_k^2\bigr)
\ge\frac{t_ks^2}{2^{n+1}}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{13}
\]
Thus \(a(s)\le 2^{n+1}F(s)/s^2\) for \(0<s\le|D|\), including all positive block endpoints with the convention (10). For \(s>|D|\) the same inequality holds because \(a(s)=0\le F(s)\). Nothing is divided by rank zero.

For an arbitrary real \(R>0\), split the integral of \(a\) at \(R\), use \(a\le b\) before \(R\), and apply (13) after \(R\). This gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
W
&\le\int_0^R b(s)\,ds
+2^{n+1}\int_R^\infty\frac1{s^2}\int_0^s b(u)\,du\,ds\\
&=\left(1+\frac{2^{n+1}}R\right)\int_0^R b(u)\,du
+\int_R^\infty\frac{2^{n+1}}u b(u)\,du.
\end{aligned}
\tag{14}
\]
To verify the equality, for fixed \(u\ge0\) the inner \(s\)-integral after interchanging order is over \(s\ge\max\{R,u\}\), with integral \(1/\max\{R,u\}\). Nonnegativity justifies the interchange, and \(R>0\) and finite support make the resulting integrals finite. In particular (14) remains valid when \(R>|D|\): the extended function \(a\) then vanishes on the tail, whereas \(F\) is allowed to be constant and positive there.

Cauchy-Schwarz applied to the right side of (14), with coefficient \(1+2^{n+1}/R\) on \([0,R]\) and coefficient \(2^{n+1}/u\) on \((R,\infty)\), proves
\[
\begin{aligned}
W^2
&\le\left[
R\left(1+\frac{2^{n+1}}R\right)^2
+\int_R^\infty\frac{2^{2n+2}}{u^2}\,du
\right]\int_0^\infty b(u)^2\,du\\
&=\left(R+4\,2^n+\frac{8\,2^{2n}}R\right)
\int_0^\infty b(u)^2\,du.
\end{aligned}
\tag{15}
\]
The scalar expression satisfies \(R+8\,2^{2n}/R\ge2\sqrt{8\,2^{2n}}=4\sqrt2\,2^n\), since \((\sqrt R-\sqrt{8\,2^{2n}/R})^2\ge0\). Equality holds at \(R=2\sqrt2\,2^n\), which is permitted regardless of the support size. With this choice, (11) and (15) yield
\[
W^2\le(4+4\sqrt2)2^n
\sum_{\mathbf j\in D}\tau_w(\mathbf j)^2.
\tag{16}
\]
The reciprocal \((4+4\sqrt2)^{-1}=(\sqrt2-1)/4\) proves (3).

All counting was in the given ambient lattice, and all halfspaces used ambient normals, so no full-rank assumption entered. In affine rank zero, nonempty \(D\) is a singleton, its supported depth is exactly its weight \(W\), and (3) holds as well. This also verifies directly the single-block, singleton situation where the chosen \(R\) exceeds the support size. For the identically zero table, the positive support is empty and both sides of (3) vanish. The positive-mass proof and probability normalizations are needed only when \(W>0\).

Because \(S_2>0\) and every weight sampled by \(\pi\) is positive, direct cancellation gives
\[
\sum_{\mathbf j\in D}\frac{w_{\mathbf j}^2}{S_2}
\left(\frac{\tau_w(\mathbf j)}{w_{\mathbf j}}\right)^2
=\frac1{S_2}\sum_{\mathbf j\in D}\tau_w(\mathbf j)^2.
\tag{17}
\]
Multiplying or dividing by \(S_2\) shows exact equivalence of (3) and the lower bound in (4). For an arbitrary probability law \(q\) on \(D\), the same expectation instead equals \(\sum_D(q_{\mathbf j}/w_{\mathbf j}^2)\tau_w(\mathbf j)^2\); the cancellation in (17) uses the specified coefficients of \(\pi\). Likewise substituting \(p=w/W\) and \(\tau_p=\tau_w/W\) gives \(\sum_Dp_{\mathbf j}\tau_p(\mathbf j)^2=W^{-3}\sum_Dw_{\mathbf j}\tau_w(\mathbf j)^2\), with the additional weight factor. These algebraic identities establish the stated distinction from the weighted H2 moment and from replacing the sampling law.

For the Boolean table, two points of \(\{0,1\}^n\) in the same parity class must coincide. Thus (1) holds for two positive endpoints, and it holds trivially if either endpoint has zero weight. At a vertex \(\mathbf j\in\{0,1\}^n\), choose the nonzero vector with components \(u_\ell=2j_\ell-1\). For any other vertex \(\mathbf i\), one has \(\mathbf u\cdot(\mathbf i-\mathbf j)=-|\{\ell:i_\ell\ne j_\ell\}|<0\). The closed halfspace through \(\mathbf j\) with normal \(\mathbf u\) therefore retains only \(\mathbf j\). The atom lower bound proves \(\tau_w(\mathbf j)=1\). Hence \(W=2^n\) and the sum of squared depths is \(2^n=W^2/2^n\). If it were always at least \(c\rho^nW^2\), this example would require \(c(2\rho)^n\le1\) for all \(n\), impossible when \(c>0\) and \(\rho>1/2\).

To check applicability to actual bodies, use only the actual-table conclusion established in the proof of accepted fact 488f0a583886b5fc: when \(W>0\), the full table \(w_{\mathbf j}=\mathcal L^d(C_{\mathbf j})\), including every zero-volume and boundary fiber, admits a finite-valued nonnegative log-concave extension \(f\) on \(\mathbb R^n\) agreeing at every lattice point. This uses exactly the same \(C_{\mathbf j},w,D,W,S,n,d\) as above. For positive same-parity endpoints, its midpoint inequality gives
\[
w_{(\mathbf i+\mathbf k)/2}
=f\left(\frac{\mathbf i+\mathbf k}{2}\right)
\ge\sqrt{w_{\mathbf i}w_{\mathbf k}}
\ge\min\{w_{\mathbf i},w_{\mathbf k}\}.
\tag{18}
\]
If either endpoint has zero weight, nonnegativity suffices for (1). Compactness of \(C\) makes the table finitely supported and all weights finite. Thus (3)-(4) apply without an extra positivity assumption on boundary fibers. The hypothesis of our abstract theorem is weaker than existence of such an extension: in \(\mathbb Z\), the table equal to one at \(0\) and \(3\), and zero elsewhere, satisfies (1), because its two positive sites have different parities. It is not complete in its convex hull, and a log-concave extension would have \(f(1)\ge f(0)^{2/3}f(3)^{1/3}=1\), contradicting its required lattice value zero. This verifies directly why completeness or log-concavity was not assumed in (8).

For \(\mathbf z=(\mathbf j,\mathbf y)\in S\) and \(\mathbf u\ne\mathbf0\), the ambient halfspace \(\{(\mathbf x,\mathbf v):\mathbf u\cdot(\mathbf x-\mathbf j)\ge0\}\) contains \(\mathbf z\) and has mixed-integer mass exactly \(\sum_{\mathbf i:\mathbf u\cdot(\mathbf i-\mathbf j)\ge0}w_{\mathbf i}\). Taking its infimum proves \(h_S(\mathbf z)\le\tau_w(\mathbf j)\). When \(W=0\), every measurable subset of \(S\) has mixed-integer volume zero, so every such depth is zero, including at points in nonempty zero-volume fibers. This covers the locked problem's zero-volume case.

Finally consider the body in (6). Write \(N=2m+1\), so \(m\ge1\), and let \(Q=[-1/2,1/2]^d\). The integer fibers are exactly \(\{i\}\times Q\) for \(i=0,\ldots,2m\); all have volume one, and every other integer fiber is empty. Its table is midpoint-quasiconcave because the integer midpoint of two points of \([0,2m]\cap\mathbb Z\) stays in that interval. In one dimension a nonzero normal has positive or negative sign. The two closed halfspaces through \(i\) give masses \(N-i\) and \(i+1\), respectively, proving the depth formula. Its squared-depth sum is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=0}^{2m}\tau_w(i)^2
&=2\sum_{k=1}^m k^2+(m+1)^2\\
&=\frac{m(m+1)(2m+1)}3+(m+1)^2\\
&=\frac{(m+1)(2m^2+4m+3)}3
=\frac{(N+1)(N^2+2N+3)}{12}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{19}
\]
For completeness, the finite square-sum identity used here follows by summing \((k+1)^3-k^3=3k^2+3k+1\) from \(k=1\) to \(m\), and using \(\sum_{k=1}^m k=m(m+1)/2\); the latter follows by pairing \(k\) with \(m+1-k\).

The point \(\mathbf z_0=(m,\mathbf0)\) belongs to \(S\). The reflection \(T(i,\mathbf y)=(2m-i,-\mathbf y)\) preserves \(S\) and its mixed-integer measure: it permutes the integer fibers and preserves their \(d\)-dimensional volumes. If \(H\) is a closed halfspace with boundary through \(\mathbf z_0\), then \(T(H)\) is its opposite closed halfspace. They cover the whole ambient space, and their intersections with \(S\) have equal measure. Consequently each has measure at least \(W/2=N/2\), regardless of any measure on the common boundary. Any halfspace containing \(\mathbf z_0\) contains such a parallel halfspace through it, so \(h_S(\mathbf z_0)\ge N/2\).

For the matching upper bound at every point \(\mathbf z=(i,\mathbf y)\in S\), use the first continuous coordinate, available because \(d\ge1\). If \(y_1\ge0\), the containing ambient halfspace \(v_1\ge y_1\) cuts from each unit cube a volume \(1/2-y_1\le1/2\). If \(y_1<0\), the containing halfspace \(v_1\le y_1\) cuts from each unit cube a volume \(y_1+1/2\le1/2\). These formulas include the cube boundary; hyperplanes of a fixed continuous coordinate have \(d\)-volume zero in each fiber. The resulting total mass is at most \(N/2\). Thus every \(h_S(\mathbf z)\le N/2\), and the center attains equality, proving (6).

The ratio that would have to be bounded below by \(c\) in (5) is therefore exactly
\[
\frac{\max_{\mathbf z\in S}h_S(\mathbf z)}
{\bigl(\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\tau_w(i)^2\bigr)/W}
=\frac{6N^2}{(N+1)(N^2+2N+3)}
<\frac6N\longrightarrow0.
\tag{20}
\]
Given any \(c>0\), choose an odd \(N\ge3\) with \(N>6/c\). Then (20) is smaller than \(c\), contradicting (5). The same exact sum is asymptotic to \(N^3/12\), whereas the maximum actual depth is \(N/2\). This obstruction holds already at the fixed integer dimension \(n=1\) and any fixed \(d\ge1\). It disproves the specified conversion while leaving the locked weak Oertel inequality unresolved.
statement:
Let \(n\ge1\) be an integer and let \(w:\mathbb Z^n\to[0,\infty)\) be a nonzero finitely supported table satisfying
\[
w_{(\mathbf i+\mathbf k)/2}\ge\min\{w_{\mathbf i},w_{\mathbf k}\}
\qquad
(\mathbf i,\mathbf k\in\mathbb Z^n,
\ \mathbf i\equiv\mathbf k\pmod2).
\tag{1}
\]
Retain the canonical positive support \(D=\{\mathbf j:w_{\mathbf j}>0\}\), total mass \(W=\sum_{\mathbf j\in D}w_{\mathbf j}>0\), and probability weights \(p_{\mathbf j}=w_{\mathbf j}/W\). For every \(\mathbf j\in\mathbb R^n\), define
\[
\tau_w(\mathbf j)
=\inf_{\mathbf u\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{\mathbf0\}}
\sum_{\substack{\mathbf i\in D\\
\mathbf u\cdot(\mathbf i-\mathbf j)\ge0}}w_{\mathbf i},
\qquad
\tau_p(\mathbf j)=\frac{\tau_w(\mathbf j)}{W}.
\tag{2}
\]
These are closed-halfspace depths of the discrete index measure, with the canonical normalization \(\tau_w=W\tau_p\). Then
\[
\sum_{\mathbf j\in D}\tau_w(\mathbf j)^2
\ge\frac{\sqrt2-1}{4}\,\frac{W^2}{2^n}.
\tag{3}
\]
With \(S_2=\sum_{\mathbf j\in D}w_{\mathbf j}^2\) and the original squared-weight law \(\pi_{\mathbf j}=w_{\mathbf j}^2/S_2\), one has the exact identity and consequently the equivalent inequality
\[
\mathbb E_{\mathbf J\sim\pi}
\left[\left(\frac{\tau_w(\mathbf J)}{w_{\mathbf J}}\right)^2\right]
=\frac1{S_2}\sum_{\mathbf j\in D}\tau_w(\mathbf j)^2
\ge\frac{\sqrt2-1}{4}\,\frac{W^2}{2^nS_2}.
\tag{4}
\]
The weight table \(w=1\) on \(D=\{0,1\}^n\), with zero elsewhere, satisfies (1) and has \(\tau_w(\mathbf j)=1\) at every supported index. Hence its left side in (3) is exactly \(W^2/2^n\). In particular, for every \(\rho>1/2\) and \(c>0\), an inequality \(\sum_D\tau_w^2\ge c\rho^nW^2\) fails for some \(n\). This establishes the sharp exponential scale, without claiming sharpness of the numerical constant in (3).

For an actual convex body \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^d\), \(d\ge1\), set \(C_{\mathbf j}=\{\mathbf y:(\mathbf j,\mathbf y)\in C\}\), \(w_{\mathbf j}=\mathcal L^d(C_{\mathbf j})\), and \(S=C\cap(\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R^d)\). Empty and lower-dimensional fibers have weight zero. Here \(W=\mathcal H_d(S)\), in the notation of the locked problem and accepted fact 488f0a583886b5fc. When \(W>0\), this full fiber table satisfies (1), so (3)-(4) apply. For every \(\mathbf z=(\mathbf j,\mathbf y)\in S\), its ambient mixed-integer depth satisfies \(h_S(\mathbf z)\le\tau_w(\mathbf j)\). If \(W=0\), the unweighted inequality reads \(0\ge0\), and \(h_S(\mathbf z)=0\) for every \(\mathbf z\in S\); the probability normalizations in (2) and (4) are not defined or asserted in this case.

There is no absolute \(c>0\) such that every such body with \(W>0\) satisfies
\[
\max_{\mathbf z\in S}h_S(\mathbf z)
\ge c\,\frac{\sum_{\mathbf j\in D}\tau_w(\mathbf j)^2}{W}.
\tag{5}
\]
More precisely, for every odd integer \(N\ge3\) and every \(d\ge1\), the full-dimensional convex body \(C=[0,N-1]\times[-1/2,1/2]^d\subset\mathbb R^{1+d}\) has exactly \(N\) positive integer fibers, all of volume one, and
\[
\begin{aligned}
W&=N,&
\tau_w(i)&=\min\{i+1,N-i\}\quad(0\le i\le N-1),\\
\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\tau_w(i)^2
&=\frac{(N+1)(N^2+2N+3)}{12},&
\max_{\mathbf z\in S}h_S(\mathbf z)&=\frac N2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{6}
\]

The degree-two unweighted sum in (3) is distinct from the degree-three weighted numerator in the normalized H2 moment \(\sum_{\mathbf j\in D}p_{\mathbf j}\tau_p(\mathbf j)^2=W^{-3}\sum_{\mathbf j\in D}w_{\mathbf j}\tau_w(\mathbf j)^2\). Equation (4) uses exactly \(\pi=w^2/S_2\) from the original table; it does not assert the same estimate after replacement by a target law \(q\) obtained by optimizing a transport. Neither an H2 bound nor the locked weak Oertel conclusion is asserted.
